title: Security review - audit logging for route experiments (Helio Finance)
summary: Helio Finance ran a security/compliance review focused on audit logging and change management for Redwood Console route-level experiments (A/B testing at routing layer). Helio asked what experiment lifecycle/config change events are logged, which fields are included (actor identity, source IP, request IDs, before/after diff), retention periods, and how audit events can be exported to their SIEM. Redwood confirmed audit events exist for create/update/start/stop/delete and RBAC denials, support SSO/SAML-based actor identity, and export via audit log export pipeline (scheduled export + API). Open items: provide sample audit event payloads (redacted), retention options for enterprise, and documentation evidence (SOC 2, audit logging spec, and data flow).
topics: Scope of audit logging for experiments (create/update/start/stop/delete, guardrail actions)
Audit event fields (actor, tenant, route/experiment IDs, change diff, IP/request ID)
Retention and immutability expectations (WORM/SIEM retention alignment)
Export options (API, scheduled export, SIEM integrations)
Data residency and where audit logs are stored/processed
Evidence requests for vendor risk review (SOC 2, docs, sample payloads)
action_items: Kevin Osei - Send Helio a redacted sample of experiment audit events (create/update/start/stop) including change diff format and required fields - Due 2025-03-21
Marcus Lin - Share SOC 2 Type II report + security overview pack and confirm audit log retention options for enterprise plan - Due 2025-03-22
Kaitlyn Nguyen - Provide RBAC permission matrix for experiment actions (create/start/stop/delete, view audit trail, export) and clarify break-glass admin flow - Due 2025-03-25
Marissa Cole - Send product note clarifying soft-stop vs optional hard-stop behavior for guardrails and what is recorded in audit trail when guardrails trigger - Due 2025-03-25
Helio (Daniel Cho) - Confirm Helio required audit log retention (e.g., 7 years) and preferred export destination (Splunk vs S3) - Due 2025-03-26
next_steps: Redwood to provide evidence pack (SOC2, audit logging spec, sample payloads) for Helio vendor risk intake
Follow-up 30 min working session with Helio Platform Eng to align on SIEM export method and required fields
Helio to confirm retention requirement and whether they need WORM storage / immutability attestations
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Date: 2025-03-19
Time: 4:00pm - 4:47pm PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Title: Security review - audit logging for route experiments (Helio Finance)

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Kaitlyn Nguyen, Marissa Cole
Helio Finance: Priya Shah, Daniel Cho, Amina El-Sayed, Rachel Kim

---
Summary (auto-generated)
- Helio reviewed audit logging requirements around route-level experiments (A/B testing) and asked for event field coverage, retention, and export mechanisms.
- Redwood described lifecycle events, RBAC enforcement, and audit export options.
- Follow-ups requested: sample audit payloads, retention policy details, and compliance evidence.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Experiment configuration changes and audit trail
2) Audit log retention and export
3) RBAC and admin controls
4) Evidence for vendor risk

Questions (auto-generated)
- Do audit logs include before/after config diffs and the actor identity from SSO?
- Can we export audit events to Splunk/SIEM and keep 7-year retention?
- Are guardrail auto-stops recorded and attributable?

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send sample payloads + docs.
- Helio to confirm retention and SIEM destination.

---
Transcript

[00:00] Marcus Lin: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Marcus, I’m on the security engineering side at Redwood. We pulled in Kevin who owns audit export, Kaitlyn for RBAC, and Marissa from product for the experiment feature.

[00:14] Priya Shah: Great. Thanks Marcus. Priya here. We’re basically doing our standard vendor risk check, but this one is specific because we’re going to allow application teams to do these… experiments in production. So we need strong change logging.

[00:30] Daniel Cho: Daniel, GRC. I’ll probably ask the annoying retention questions.

[00:34] Rachel Kim: Rachel from vendor risk. I’m mainly tracking evidence requests.

[00:39] Amina El-Sayed: Hi, Amina, platform engineering. I want to understand what we can actually see and export.

[00:45] Marcus Lin: Perfect. Quick agenda: we’ll cover (1) what actions generate audit events for route experiments, (2) what fields we include, (3) retention and export options, and (4) evidence we can provide. Sound good?

[00:58] Priya Shah: Yep.

[01:00] Marcus Lin: Great. Marissa, do you want to do a thirty-second overview of the feature so we’re all aligned?

[01:05] Marissa Cole: Sure. Route experiments let you define an A/B/n test on a route—so like a specific endpoint or traffic policy—and split traffic deterministically between variants. Variants typically map to model versions or different routing configs. It’s operated in Console, with guardrails for latency, error rate, and cost, and optional quality signals from our eval pipeline.

[01:30] Priya Shah: Okay. The key thing for us: any config change that could affect where traffic goes has to be auditable.

[01:37] Marcus Lin: Yep. That’s exactly the intention. So: audit events. We generate events for experiment lifecycle operations: create experiment, update experiment config, start, stop, delete. Also we log changes to allocations—traffic split changes—eligibility rules, route bindings, and guardrail threshold changes.

[02:01] Amina El-Sayed: When you say update, is it like any field change? Or only some fields?

[02:06] Marcus Lin: It’s any mutation to the experiment object in the control plane. Kaitlyn can add detail, but our API layer enforces RBAC and writes an audit event with a diff summary.

[02:16] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yeah. From the Console API perspective, all experiment mutations go through a single service. We capture the actor identity, the action, the resource identifiers, and a “change summary” that includes before/after for the fields that changed.

[02:33] Daniel Cho: Before/after like the whole JSON? Or…?

[02:36] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Not the full blob by default. It’s a structured diff in the sense of “field path changed from X to Y”. For large fields we truncate. We also redact secrets—though experiments generally don’t have secrets.

[02:49] Priya Shah: I’ll be direct: we need to show an auditor that if someone changed the routing split from 10% to 50% we can see who did it, when, and what it was before.

[02:59] Marcus Lin: Yes, that’s supported.

[03:01] Priya Shah: And it needs to be tied to their SSO identity.

[03:05] Kaitlyn Nguyen: We support SSO/SAML for Console. The audit event has both an internal actor ID and the external identity attributes (like email, and if present, the SAML subject). If a token is used, it’s the service account identity.

[03:20] Daniel Cho: Do you capture IP address?

[03:23] Kaitlyn Nguyen: For Console actions, yes: source IP as seen at the edge. Also user agent. For API keys, we capture the API key ID, not the secret.

[03:34] Amina El-Sayed: Request IDs too? For correlation?

[03:37] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yep. request_id and trace_id if the request is traced through our system. It’s helpful for incident response.

[03:44] Priya Shah: Good.

[03:46] Rachel Kim: Can you list the exact event types? Like names.

[03:50] Kevin Osei: We can send the canonical list. Off the top of my head, they’re along the lines of EXPERIMENT_CREATED, EXPERIMENT_UPDATED, EXPERIMENT_STARTED, EXPERIMENT_STOPPED, EXPERIMENT_DELETED. There’s also RBAC_DENIED events for sensitive actions in some tiers.

[04:08] Marcus Lin: And for clarity, there are also audit events for exporting audit logs—so if someone triggers an export job, that is itself auditable.

[04:16] Daniel Cho: That’s good. Now retention: what’s default retention of the audit logs on your side?

[04:23] Marcus Lin: In our standard enterprise offering we retain audit events for at least one year in the Console, and export is available. We can extend retention depending on the plan.

[04:35] Daniel Cho: We require seven years for certain systems. Not necessarily you holding it for seven, but we need a reliable export mechanism that we can put into our archival.

[04:45] Kevin Osei: Understood. The pattern we see is customers export to their SIEM or an archive bucket on a schedule—daily or hourly—and then you retain it as long as you need. We support scheduled export and API-based retrieval.

[05:01] Amina El-Sayed: Export as… what format?

[05:04] Kevin Osei: JSON lines. One event per line. We can also provide CSV for some consumers, but JSONL is the canonical.

[05:12] Priya Shah: Do you have Splunk integration?

[05:16] Kevin Osei: We don’t have a “click a button Splunk app” in this feature yet. But we can deliver to S3 or a customer-controlled bucket and you can ingest from there. Some customers also use HTTP event collector patterns; we can discuss, but the supported path today is export to storage + ingestion on your side.

[05:36] Rachel Kim: So you’re saying S3. Is it your S3 or ours?

[05:40] Kevin Osei: Typically a Redwood-managed export location with a secure link, or customer-provided bucket with cross-account role. For regulated accounts, we usually do customer-owned bucket.

[05:52] Priya Shah: We’d want customer-owned.

[05:54] Kevin Osei: Yep.

[05:56] Daniel Cho: And encryption at rest? KMS?

[06:00] Kevin Osei: In the customer-owned bucket case, you control the KMS key policy. On our side, our storage is encrypted at rest. For customer-owned, we can assume a role with least privilege to write objects.

[06:14] Priya Shah: Do you support object lock? Like WORM?

[06:18] Kevin Osei: We don’t enforce object lock ourselves, but if your bucket has object lock enabled, we’ll write objects and your retention policy will apply. We can document that.

[06:29] Daniel Cho: Okay. Next: content. What exact fields are in an audit event? Not hand-wavy.

[06:35] Marcus Lin: We can provide a sample payload, but verbally: event_id, event_type, timestamp, organization_id (tenant), actor (user id/email), auth type, source_ip, user_agent, resource type and resource identifiers (experiment_id, route_id), action result (success/denied), and change summary.

[06:57] Priya Shah: Does it include variant IDs?

[06:59] Marcus Lin: Yes when relevant. For example if you update allocations or swap a model binding for a variant, the diff will include variant_id and the changed fields.

[07:09] Amina El-Sayed: And does it include the model ID? Like “we changed variant B from model X to model Y”?

[07:15] Marissa Cole: Yes, that’s part of the config. And the audit diff captures that. The model IDs are first-class fields.

[07:24] Priya Shah: Great. What about guardrails. If a guardrail triggers and auto-stops an experiment, is that audited?

[07:31] Marissa Cole: There are two behaviors: soft-stop where we notify and mark degraded, and optional hard-stop for severe regressions. When a stop is triggered automatically, we record the action as a system-initiated stop with the trigger reason, like p99 latency regression threshold.

[07:49] Daniel Cho: “System-initiated” actor is like a service account?

[07:53] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Exactly. It’s a system principal, and the event includes the trigger metadata and the evaluation window.

[08:02] Priya Shah: I need that. Because otherwise it’s like, “why did traffic change.”

[08:07] Marcus Lin: Totally.

[08:09] Amina El-Sayed: Small nuance: Does stopping drain traffic or is it instant? Because from a control standpoint, auditors care less, but operations cares.

[08:18] Marissa Cole: For stop semantics, it’s effectively immediate in routing once configs propagate, but there’s propagation lag bounds. We show status transitions in Console. It’s not like a 2-hour drain, it’s more like within minutes.

[08:32] Priya Shah: That leads to another question: do you audit the propagation? Like config versioning?

[08:37] Marcus Lin: We audit the configuration change itself, including a config version number. Separately, we have telemetry for propagation lag, but we don’t emit an “audit event” for every propagation step—more like metrics.

[08:53] Daniel Cho: Okay. We may ask for those metrics during incident investigations but it’s not an audit control.

[09:00] Rachel Kim: Evidence-wise, we’ll need documentation that describes the audit logging system and a sample export.

[09:08] Marcus Lin: Understood. We have an audit logging spec for experiments and can share it under NDA. We can also provide a redacted sample of JSONL export.

[09:18] Priya Shah: Another thing: Are audit logs immutable? Like can an admin delete them?

[09:23] Marcus Lin: In our system, customers cannot delete audit events. Redwood has restricted internal access with break-glass controls. For your compliance posture, we recommend exporting to your immutable store.

[09:37] Daniel Cho: We will. But do you log break-glass access?

[09:41] Marcus Lin: Yes, privileged access is itself audited internally. We can provide a statement in the security doc; we usually don’t share raw internal audit logs, but we can describe the controls.

[09:53] Priya Shah: Fine.

[09:55] Amina El-Sayed: RBAC: who can start/stop experiments? Can we restrict that to a platform admin role?

[10:02] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes. There are granular permissions: create experiment, update config, start, stop, delete, view results, view audit trail, export audit. You can map those to roles in your org. And we support SSO group-to-role mapping.

[10:19] Priya Shah: Good. Do you support approvals? Like two-person rule?

[10:24] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Not built-in for this release. Some customers implement that process externally via their change management, and then only allow a limited group to execute the action.

[10:36] Daniel Cho: Understood. So no native workflow approvals.

[10:39] Marissa Cole: Correct, not yet.

[10:41] Priya Shah: Next question: can we export audit logs via API to pull into our GRC system?

[10:48] Kevin Osei: Yes. There’s an API to query audit events with filtering by time window and resource. For high volume we recommend the scheduled export. Also pagination, obviously.

[11:02] Amina El-Sayed: What about rate limits?

[11:05] Kevin Osei: There are standard limits; for enterprise we can raise. But again, exports are better.

[11:12] Daniel Cho: Is there a way to prove completeness? Like “we didn’t miss events.”

[11:17] Kevin Osei: We include monotonically increasing sequence numbers per tenant in the export stream, and the export job reports counts. If there is a gap, you can detect it. We can walk through details when we send the docs.

[11:33] Priya Shah: That’s actually really helpful.

[11:35] Rachel Kim: Do you have a SOC 2 Type II?

[11:39] Marcus Lin: Yes.

[11:41] Rachel Kim: And that would cover change management and logging controls?

[11:45] Marcus Lin: It covers relevant trust service criteria, including logging/monitoring controls at the platform level. For this feature-specific audit logging, we’ll provide the feature documentation plus the sample payloads.

[11:58] Daniel Cho: Okay. Switching gears a bit—data residency. If our account is in US region, where are audit logs stored and processed?

[12:07] Marcus Lin: For hosted Console, audit events are stored with the control plane data. We can discuss region-specific storage; in general, we align data residency to the selected region for enterprise accounts, but exports can be to your bucket in your chosen region.

[12:23] Priya Shah: We require US-only. No EU processing.

[12:27] Marcus Lin: That’s standard for many customers. We can confirm in writing based on your deployment plan.

[12:34] Amina El-Sayed: Is this the hosted control plane or do you offer private control plane?

[12:39] Marissa Cole: We offer private deployments as well. For this conversation we’re assuming hosted + dedicated capacity, but private is an option if you need more isolation.

[12:51] Priya Shah: For now we’re assessing hosted but with strict controls.

[12:56] Marcus Lin: Got it.

[12:58] Daniel Cho: Okay, can you walk through an example event? Like “update experiment allocation from 5/95 to 50/50.”

[13:07] Kevin Osei: Sure. It would show event_type EXPERIMENT_UPDATED, resource experiment_id=exp_123, route_id=route_abc, actor_email=jane@helio.com, source_ip, then change_summary: allocations.variantA from 0.05 to 0.50, allocations.variantB from 0.95 to 0.50, plus a config_version increment.

[13:30] Priya Shah: And timestamp in UTC?

[13:32] Kevin Osei: Yes, ISO timestamp.

[13:35] Daniel Cho: And you mentioned redaction. What gets redacted?

[13:39] Marcus Lin: We redact anything classified as secret. For experiments, it’s mostly not applicable. Potentially user-provided notes could be partially redacted if it includes tokens or credentials, but that’s more of a general rule.

[13:55] Priya Shah: Okay.

[13:56] Amina El-Sayed: Can audit events include the “eligibility rule” changes? Like if we decide to bucket by customer ID vs session.

[14:04] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes, changes to eligibility and stickiness key selection are captured. The change summary would say stickiness_key from “customer_id” to “header:X-Helio-User” or similar.

[14:20] Priya Shah: That’s a sensitive one for us. Because if someone changes stickiness to something low entropy you can skew traffic.

[14:28] Marissa Cole: We actually added validations and warnings in Console around missing or low-entropy stickiness keys. But yes, it’s audited.

[14:37] Daniel Cho: Validations are nice, but audit is required.

[14:41] Marcus Lin: Agreed.

[14:44] Priya Shah: Another question: do you log read access? Like someone viewing audit logs.

[14:51] Kevin Osei: We log export initiation and some sensitive reads depending on the tier. For general “view audit events” in Console, we can confirm whether it’s logged as an access event. It’s not always on by default.

[15:06] Priya Shah: We want it. At least for export and for permission changes.

[15:10] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Permission changes are definitely audited.

[15:12] Marcus Lin: We’ll take that as a follow-up: confirm read-audit behavior and what’s available.

[15:19] Rachel Kim: Please.

[15:21] Daniel Cho: What about integration with our SIEM. If it’s S3 export, how quickly can we get events? Near-real time?

[15:30] Kevin Osei: It’s not streaming real time today. It’s scheduled. Hourly is common, sometimes every 15 minutes depending on volume. For vendor risk, we usually position it as “export within an hour.” If you need sub-minute, we’d need to scope.

[15:48] Priya Shah: An hour is okay for audit. Not okay for detection, but we have other signals.

[15:54] Marcus Lin: Right. For detection/monitoring, we also provide operational alerts and metrics for guardrails and propagation lag. Those are separate from audit logs.

[16:05] Amina El-Sayed: Do those alerts include a link to what changed?

[16:09] Marissa Cole: In Console, guardrail banners can link to the audit history for the experiment. In alerts, we can include the experiment ID and runbook link. But not always the exact diff.

[16:23] Priya Shah: Okay.

[16:25] Daniel Cho: Now I’m going to ask a compliance-y question. Is the audit log tamper-evident? Like hashed chain.

[16:33] Marcus Lin: We don’t provide a cryptographic hash chain for audit events today. We rely on access controls and export to customer-controlled immutability. If that’s a hard requirement, we should flag it.

[16:48] Daniel Cho: It’s not hard. But we will ask how you prevent modification.

[16:53] Marcus Lin: Understood. We can document the controls: append-only storage pattern on our side, no customer deletion, and privileged access controls.

[17:05] Rachel Kim: We’ll need that documented, yes.

[17:08] Priya Shah: And about who at Redwood can see our audit logs.

[17:12] Marcus Lin: Default is no routine access. For support escalations, limited on-call roles can access with break-glass approval. Access is logged.

[17:24] Priya Shah: Good.

[17:26] Amina El-Sayed: I want to ask about the debug endpoint you mentioned in a previous email—like explaining assignment decisions. Is that accessible to customers?

[17:36] Marissa Cole: The assignment debug endpoint is internal by default. For customers, we provide variant headers in responses and Console views. If we expose debug tools, it would be gated and heavily redacted.

[17:50] Priya Shah: Okay, please don’t expose anything that leaks identifiers.

[17:54] Marcus Lin: Understood.

[17:56] Daniel Cho: When you export audit logs, do you include customer PII in them? Like user IDs.

[18:02] Kevin Osei: We include actor identity for the person making the change, which in your case is your employee email. We don’t include end-user identifiers unless you put them into the experiment config, which you shouldn’t.

[18:18] Priya Shah: Okay, so normal admin action logs.

[18:21] Kevin Osei: Exactly.

[18:23] Rachel Kim: Are there sub-processors involved for audit logging?

[18:28] Marcus Lin: For hosted Console, yes, but we can provide the subprocessor list as part of the security pack. The audit events are part of our core control plane; we’ll detail where they’re stored.

[18:40] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[18:42] Priya Shah: Let’s talk about “export scope.” We need all audit events for our tenant, not only experiments.

[18:49] Kevin Osei: Yes, export can include all audit categories. Experiments are one category. If you want to filter just experiment events, you can.

[19:01] Amina El-Sayed: Can we scope to a specific project or environment? Like prod vs staging.

[19:06] Kevin Osei: If you have separate tenants/environments, yes. Within a tenant, we include environment tags where applicable.

[19:15] Priya Shah: Another question: if an experiment is created via API vs Console UI, same audit?

[19:21] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Same. It’s the same service.

[19:24] Daniel Cho: What about failed attempts? Like someone tries to start an experiment and gets denied.

[19:29] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Denied actions are logged as well in our security audit trail. At least for sensitive mutations.

[19:38] Priya Shah: Perfect.

[19:40] Marcus Lin: Are there any specific fields Helio requires that we haven’t mentioned? Sometimes customers ask for geo, device, etc.

[19:49] Daniel Cho: Mainly: actor, time, action, resource, before/after, and outcome. Also correlation ID.

[19:58] Priya Shah: And if possible, “reason.” Like guardrail stop reason.

[20:02] Marissa Cole: Yep. That’s included for system-triggered actions.

[20:06] Rachel Kim: For evidence, we’ll need: security whitepaper, SOC2, pen test summary if available, data retention policy, and these audit log samples.

[20:16] Marcus Lin: We can provide SOC2 and the security overview. Pen test summary depends, but we usually can provide an attestation letter or executive summary. We’ll follow up.

[20:28] Priya Shah: Also any doc specific to experiment audit logs.

[20:31] Kevin Osei: We have a spec doc for experiment-config audit events. We’ll send it.

[20:36] Amina El-Sayed: On the product side, can we export from Console UI or only API?

[20:41] Kevin Osei: Both. There’s a UI for admins to configure export, and an API.

[20:48] Priya Shah: Does that UI action itself get audited?

[20:51] Kevin Osei: Yes, export configuration changes are audited.

[20:55] Priya Shah: Great.

[20:57] Daniel Cho: Let’s talk about retention in Console UI. You said one year. Is that hard-coded?

[21:03] Marcus Lin: It depends on plan. Default is one year visible in Console for enterprise; longer retention can be negotiated, but again we recommend export for 7-year. We’ll confirm exact numbers for your proposed plan.

[21:20] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[21:22] Priya Shah: Can you confirm if audit log data is included in backups, and how long backups retain it.

[21:30] Marcus Lin: It is included in backups per our standard. Backup retention is shorter and is not intended as compliance retention. We can provide the policy in the security pack.

[21:44] Priya Shah: Okay.

[21:46] Amina El-Sayed: I want to ask about “quality” evals. If the experiment has eval hooks, does that change what’s in audit logs?

[21:54] Marissa Cole: Not much. If you change which eval suite is attached or the sampling rate, that’s a config change and would be audited. The eval results themselves are telemetry/analytics, not audit.

[22:08] Priya Shah: Good.

[22:10] Daniel Cho: Okay. Switching to competitor: we’ve looked at Bedrock model endpoints and Vertex. One thing they do is CloudTrail or Cloud Audit Logs. We need something roughly comparable.

[22:21] Marcus Lin: Understood. Our audit logs are similar conceptually: admin actions and configuration changes, exportable to your SIEM. We’re not claiming full CloudTrail parity, but for the experiment feature, the coverage is there.

[22:36] Priya Shah: That’s fine.

[22:38] Rachel Kim: What are the next steps? I need a timeline for receiving docs.

[22:44] Marcus Lin: Let’s do this: Kevin will send sample payloads and the event type list by Friday. I’ll send the SOC2 and security pack by Saturday. Kaitlyn will send the RBAC matrix early next week. Marissa will send a note clarifying guardrail stop behavior and audit logging around it.

[23:08] Rachel Kim: Perfect.

[23:10] Priya Shah: Can we also get a data flow diagram? Even high-level.

[23:14] Marcus Lin: Yes, we can provide a high-level architecture diagram showing Console -> control plane -> audit storage -> export pipeline.

[23:24] Amina El-Sayed: Also, do you have a way to test this in a sandbox? Like can we see sample audit entries in a demo account.

[23:31] Marissa Cole: We can set up a non-prod tenant for you as part of the POC. But for the audit export setup, we’d need to coordinate credentials for your bucket.

[23:43] Priya Shah: Okay.

[23:45] Daniel Cho: One more. When you say “change diff,” is it machine-readable? We want to ingest and run controls on it.

[23:53] Kevin Osei: It’s machine-readable. It’s basically an array of changed fields, old value, new value. Some values may be truncated. We can include a “full_config_hash” so you can verify integrity, even if values are truncated.

[24:12] Daniel Cho: Nice.

[24:14] Priya Shah: Any chance you can include “approval ticket id” in audit logs? We have ServiceNow.

[24:21] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Not first-class. But you can include an optional “change_note” field when executing the action. Some customers paste a ticket number there. That field would be captured in the audit event.

[24:34] Priya Shah: That works.

[24:36] Rachel Kim: Please note that in the docs you send.

[24:39] Marcus Lin: Will do.

[24:41] Amina El-Sayed: While we have you: do you log when someone changes RBAC roles in your system?

[24:48] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes. Role assignments and permission changes are audited with actor and before/after.

[24:56] Priya Shah: Great.

[24:58] Daniel Cho: Okay, I think we covered audit logs. Anything else you want to add?

[25:03] Marcus Lin: Just one: if your main concern is being able to reconstruct “who changed routing and when,” experiments are well covered. Separately, we also have normal rollout features (canaries, fallbacks) and those have audit as well. If you want the combined list, we can provide.

[25:22] Priya Shah: Yes, please. We care about all route-level policy changes.

[25:26] Kevin Osei: Noted.

[25:28] Rachel Kim: I’ll summarize the evidence list in email.

[25:32] Marcus Lin: Great.

[25:34] (crosstalk)

[25:35] Priya Shah: Sorry, one last question, I promise. If an experiment is deleted, can you still see its audit history?

[25:42] Kevin Osei: Yes. The resource may be deleted, but the audit events remain, and they still reference the experiment_id and route_id, plus the last known name.

[25:52] Priya Shah: Perfect.

[25:54] Daniel Cho: Okay, I’m done.

[25:57] Marcus Lin: Alright. Then we’ll do next steps: we’ll send the docs by the dates mentioned. Can we schedule a 30-minute follow-up with Amina’s team on export configuration and required fields?

[26:09] Amina El-Sayed: Yes. Next week works.

[26:12] Rachel Kim: I’ll coordinate times.

[26:14] Marcus Lin: Great. Thanks everyone.

[26:17] Priya Shah: Thanks.

[26:18] Daniel Cho: Thanks.

[26:20] Fireflies.ai transcription note: Meeting ended; some side conversation may not be captured.
